legend: Lee couldn't sleep lately, because he had nightmares. In one of his nightmares (which was about an unbalanced global round), he decided to fight back and propose a problem below (which you should solve) to balance the round, hopefully setting him free from the nightmares.
A non-empty array b1,b2,…,bm%%ZSMJ0%% is called good, if there exist m%%ZSMJ1%% integer sequences which satisfy the following properties:

The i%%ZSMJ2%%-th sequence consists of bi%%ZSMJ3%% consecutive integers (for example if bi=3%%ZSMJ4%% then the i%%ZSMJ5%%-th sequence can be (−1,0,1)%%ZSMJ6%% or (−5,−4,−3)%%ZSMJ7%% but not (0,−1,1)%%ZSMJ8%% or (1,2,3,4)%%ZSMJ9%%).
Assuming the sum of integers in the i%%ZSMJ10%%-th sequence is sumi%%ZSMJ11%%, we want sum1+sum2+…+summ%%ZSMJ12%% to be equal to 0%%ZSMJ13%%.
You are given an array a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ14%%. It has 2n−1%%ZSMJ15%% nonempty subsequences. Find how many of them are good.
As this number can be very large, output it modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ16%%.
An array c%%ZSMJ17%% is a subsequence of an array d%%ZSMJ18%% if c%%ZSMJ19%% can be obtained from d%%ZSMJ20%% by deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements.
input: The first line contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ21%% (2≤n≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ22%%) — the size of array a%%ZSMJ23%%.
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ24%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ25%% (1≤ai≤109%%ZSMJ26%%) — elements of the array.
output: Print a single integer — the number of nonempty good subsequences of a%%ZSMJ27%%, modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ28%%.
note: For the first test, two examples of good subsequences are [2,7]%%ZSMJ29%% and [2,2,4,7]%%ZSMJ30%%:

For b=[2,7]%%ZSMJ31%% we can use (−3,−4)%%ZSMJ32%% as the first sequence and (−2,−1,…,4)%%ZSMJ33%% as the second. Note that subsequence [2,7]%%ZSMJ34%% appears twice in [2,2,4,7]%%ZSMJ35%%, so we have to count it twice.
For b=[2,2,4,7]%%ZSMJ38%% the following sequences would satisfy the properties: (−1,0)%%ZSMJ39%%, (−3,−2)%%ZSMJ40%%, (0,1,2,3)%%ZSMJ41%% and (−3,−2,…,3)%%ZSMJ42%%
